subproblem.title: Derivatives of two functions agreeing on a Borel set coincide at almost every point of the set
subproblem.statement: Assume (DD), the frozen statement of the sibling node density_directions of the node being decomposed (Lean dor_lmbsf_density_directions): for every d ∈ ℕ, every Z ⊆ ℝ^d and every y ∈ ℝ^d with L^d(Z ∩ B̄_r(y))/L^d(B̄_r(y)) → 1 as r ↓ 0 (L^d = volume on Euclid d as an outer measure, B̄_r(y) = closedBall y r), and every v ∈ ℝ^d with |v| = 1, there is a sequence (y_i) in Z ∖ {y} with y_i → y and (y_i − y)/|y_i − y| → v. Let d ∈ ℕ, Z ⊆ ℝ^d Borel, and v₁, v₂ : ℝ^d → ℝ with v₁ = v₂ on Z. Then for L^d-a.e. y: if y ∈ Z and v₁, v₂ are both differentiable at y, then Dv₁(y) = Dv₂(y) (Fréchet derivatives).
subproblem.lean_statement: (∀ (d : ℕ) (Z : Set (Euclid d)) (y : Euclid d), Tendsto (fun r => volume (Z ∩ closedBall y r) / volume (closedBall y r)) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 1) → ∀ v : Euclid d, ‖v‖ = 1 → ∃ ys : ℕ → Euclid d, (∀ i, ys i ∈ Z ∧ ys i ≠ y) ∧ Tendsto ys atTop (𝓝 y) ∧ Tendsto (fun i => ‖ys i - y‖⁻¹ • (ys i - y)) atTop (𝓝 v)) → ∀ (d : ℕ) (Z : Set (Euclid d)) (v₁ v₂ : Euclid d → ℝ), MeasurableSet Z → EqOn v₁ v₂ Z → ∀ᵐ y ∂(volume : Measure (Euclid d)), y ∈ Z → DifferentiableAt ℝ v₁ y → DifferentiableAt ℝ v₂ y → fderiv ℝ v₁ y = fderiv ℝ v₂ y
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Step 4(a), the agreement lemma at density points.

1. Lebesgue density. By the Besicovitch density theorem (Besicovitch.ae_tendsto_measure_inter_div for the locally finite measure L^d, valid for an arbitrary set Z), L^d(Z ∩ B̄_r(y))/L^d(B̄_r(y)) → 1 as r ↓ 0 for (L^d⌞Z)-a.e. y. Since Z is measurable, this is equivalent to: for L^d-a.e. y, if y ∈ Z then the ratio tends to 1 (ae_restrict_iff').
2. Fix y in this full-measure set with y ∈ Z, such that v₁ and v₂ are differentiable at y. Put v := v₁ − v₂ and L := Dv₁(y) − Dv₂(y). Then v is differentiable at y with derivative L, and v = 0 on Z; in particular v(y) = 0.
3. L vanishes on unit vectors. Let |e| = 1.
 - By (DD) applied to (d, Z, y) and e, there are y_i ∈ Z with y_i ≠ y, y_i → y and q_i := |y_i − y|⁻¹(y_i − y) → e.
 - Put c_i := |y_i − y|⁻¹ and δ_i := y_i − y. Then δ_i → 0 and c_iδ_i = q_i → e.
 - By the sequential characterization of the derivative (Mathlib HasFDerivWithinAt.lim, applied within the whole space), c_i(v(y + δ_i) − v(y)) → L(e).
 - But y + δ_i = y_i ∈ Z, so v(y + δ_i) − v(y) = 0 − 0 = 0 for every i. The constant sequence 0 therefore converges to L(e), so L(e) = 0.
4. L = 0. L(0) = 0. For x ≠ 0, the vector e := |x|⁻¹x is a unit vector, so 0 = L(e) = |x|⁻¹L(x) and L(x) = 0. (If d = 0, every x equals 0.) Hence Dv₁(y) = Dv₂(y).
5. Steps 2–4 hold at every point of the full-measure set of step 1, which proves the claim. ∎

subproblem.title: Continuous left-inverse field for the derivative of a C¹ immersion
subproblem.statement: Let P, d ∈ ℕ, V ⊆ ℝ^d open and ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P C¹ on V with Dψ(y) injective for every y ∈ V. Then there is a map R : ℝ^d → L(ℝ^P, ℝ^d), continuous on V, with R(y)∘Dψ(y) = id_{ℝ^d} for every y ∈ V.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P d : ℕ) (V : Set (Euclid d)) (ψ : Euclid d → Euclid P), IsOpen V → ContDiffOn ℝ 1 ψ V → (∀ y ∈ V, Injective (fderiv ℝ ψ y)) → ∃ R : Euclid d → (Euclid P →L[ℝ] Euclid d), ContinuousOn R V ∧ ∀ y ∈ V, (R y).comp (fderiv ℝ ψ y) = ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ (Euclid d)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Step 2, “The chart field” (E(y) := Γ(y)⁻¹A(y)ᵀW(ψ(y)) with A = Dψ and Γ = AᵀA).

1. A(y) := Dψ(y) is continuous on V as a map into L(ℝ^d, ℝ^P), because ψ is C¹ on the open set V (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen).
2. The adjoint T ↦ T* : L(ℝ^d, ℝ^P) → L(ℝ^P, ℝ^d) is a linear isometry, hence continuous, and composition of operators is continuous. So y ↦ A(y)* and y ↦ Γ(y) := A(y)*∘A(y) are continuous on V.
3. Γ(y) is invertible for y ∈ V. If Γ(y)z = 0, then 0 = ⟨Γ(y)z, z⟩ = ⟨A(y)z, A(y)z⟩ = |A(y)z|², so A(y)z = 0 and z = 0 by injectivity of A(y). Thus Γ(y) is an injective linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space ℝ^d. It is therefore bijective, hence a unit of the Banach algebra L(ℝ^d, ℝ^d) (ContinuousLinearMap.isUnit_iff_bijective).
4. Let inv be the ring inverse on L(ℝ^d, ℝ^d) (Ring.inverse). It is continuous at every unit (NormedRing.inverse_continuousAt; L(ℝ^d, ℝ^d) is complete). By steps 2–3, y ↦ inv(Γ(y)) is continuous on V.
5. Define R(y) := inv(Γ(y))∘A(y)* for every y. By steps 2 and 4, R is continuous on V.
6. For y ∈ V: R(y)∘A(y) = inv(Γ(y))∘(A(y)*∘A(y)) = inv(Γ(y))∘Γ(y) = id, because Γ(y) is a unit (Ring.inverse_mul_cancel). ∎

Then there exist an open set O ⊇ C, a constant K ≥ 0 and functions u_k, u : ℝ^d → ℝ, all K-Lipschitz on ℝ^d, such that u_k → u uniformly on ℝ^d, u_k = h_k∘ψ on O for every k, and u = h∘ψ on O.

Here the cut-off multiplies the functions, u_k := χ·(h_k∘ψ), instead of taking McShane extensions. This yields global uniform convergence directly.

1. Trivial case. If C = ∅, take O = ∅, K = 0 and u_k = u = 0. Otherwise fix y₀ ∈ C. Since ‖Dh_0(0)‖ ≤ c, we have c ≥ 0.
2. Neighbourhoods. Choose δ > 0 with S := cthickening(δ, C) ⊆ V (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open). S is compact, being the closed thickening of a compact set in ℝ^d, and y₀ ∈ S. Put O := thickening(δ/2, C); O is open and contains C.
3. Cut-off. The closed sets (thickening(δ, C))ᶜ and cthickening(δ/2, C) are disjoint, since cthickening(δ/2, C) ⊆ thickening(δ, C). By the smooth Urysohn lemma (exists_contDiff_zero_iff_one_iff_of_isClosed) there is a C¹ function χ : ℝ^d → [0, 1] with χ = 0 exactly on (thickening(δ, C))ᶜ and χ = 1 exactly on cthickening(δ/2, C). Then support χ ⊆ thickening(δ, C), so tsupport χ ⊆ S ⊆ V and χ has compact support. Also χ = 1 on O.
4. Constants.
 (i) Dχ is continuous with compact support, so ‖Dχ‖ ≤ M_χ on ℝ^d.
 (ii) Dψ is continuous on the open set V, so ‖Dψ‖ ≤ M_ψ on the compact S ⊆ V.
 (iii) Each h_k is c-Lipschitz (mean value inequality from ‖Dh_k‖ ≤ c). The set ψ(S) is compact because ψ is continuous on S, so it lies in a closed ball B̄_D(ψ(y₀)). The real sequence |h_k(ψ(y₀))| converges to |h(ψ(y₀))|, so it is bounded by some B₀. For y ∈ S, |h_k(ψ(y))| ≤ |h_k(ψ(y₀))| + c|ψ(y) − ψ(y₀)| ≤ B₀ + cD =: B.
 M_χ, M_ψ and B bound norms at y₀, so they are ≥ 0. Put K := B·M_χ + c·M_ψ ≥ 0.
5. Definitions. u_k(y) := χ(y)·h_k(ψ(y)) and u(y) := χ(y)·h(ψ(y)). Since χ = 1 on O, u_k = h_k∘ψ and u = h∘ψ on O.
6. Each u_k is differentiable everywhere with ‖Du_k‖ ≤ K.
 - If y ∈ tsupport χ, then y ∈ S ⊆ V. Since V is open, ψ is differentiable at y, and h_k is differentiable at ψ(y). By the product and chain rules, Du_k(y) = χ(y)·(Dh_k(ψ(y))∘Dψ(y)) + h_k(ψ(y))·Dχ(y). Hence ‖Du_k(y)‖ ≤ 1·c·M_ψ + B·M_χ = K.
 - If y ∉ tsupport χ, then χ vanishes on the open neighbourhood (tsupport χ)ᶜ of y. So does u_k, and Du_k(y) = 0.
7. By the mean value inequality on the convex space ℝ^d, each u_k is K-Lipschitz (lipschitzWith_of_nnnorm_fderiv_le).
8. Uniform convergence. For every y, |u(y) − u_k(y)| = χ(y)·|h(ψ(y)) − h_k(ψ(y))| ≤ sup_x |h(x) − h_k(x)|. This tends to 0 because h_k → h uniformly on ℝ^P.
9. u is K-Lipschitz: |u(x) − u(z)| = lim_k |u_k(x) − u_k(z)| ≤ K|x − z|.

subproblem.title: Weak convergence of derivatives of uniformly Lipschitz, uniformly convergent functions against C¹ compactly supported test fields
subproblem.statement: Let d ∈ ℕ and K ≥ 0. Let u_k : ℝ^d → ℝ (k ∈ ℕ) be K-Lipschitz functions converging uniformly on ℝ^d to u : ℝ^d → ℝ, and let Ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d be C¹ with compact support. Write Dv(y) for the Fréchet derivative (fderiv) of v at y, which is 0 where v is not differentiable, and use Lebesgue measure on ℝ^d (volume on Euclid d) and Bochner integrals. Then ∫ Du_k(y)[Ψ(y)] dy → ∫ Du(y)[Ψ(y)] dy as k → ∞.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (d : ℕ) (K : NNReal) (us : ℕ → Euclid d → ℝ) (u : Euclid d → ℝ) (Ψ : Euclid d → Euclid d), (∀ k, LipschitzWith K (us k)) → TendstoUniformly us u atTop → ContDiff ℝ 1 Ψ → HasCompactSupport Ψ → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ y, fderiv ℝ (us k) y (Ψ y)) atTop (𝓝 (∫ y, fderiv ℝ u y (Ψ y)))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Step 3, “Integration by parts” (Simon Ch. 6, proof of 4.5(2)), specialized to globally Lipschitz functions.

1. The limit u is K-Lipschitz. For x, z ∈ ℝ^d, uniform convergence gives u_k(x) → u(x) and u_k(z) → u(z). So |u(x) − u(z)| = lim_k |u_k(x) − u_k(z)| ≤ K|x − z|. In particular u is continuous.
2. Derivative bounds and measurability. If v : ℝ^d → ℝ is C-Lipschitz, then ‖Dv(y)‖ ≤ C for every y. At points of differentiability this is the Lipschitz bound for the derivative (norm_fderiv_le_of_lipschitz); elsewhere Dv(y) = 0. For each fixed e ∈ ℝ^d, y ↦ Dv(y)[e] is Borel measurable (measurable_fderiv_apply_const).
3. Coordinates. Let e_1, …, e_d be the standard basis of ℝ^d and Ψ_l(y) := Ψ(y)_l. Then Ψ(y) = Σ_l Ψ_l(y) e_l, so Λ(Ψ(y)) = Σ_l Λ(e_l) Ψ_l(y) for every linear functional Λ. Each Ψ_l is Ψ composed with a continuous linear coordinate map, hence C¹. Since support Ψ_l ⊆ support Ψ, Ψ_l has compact support. A C¹ function with compact support has bounded derivative, so Ψ_l is Lipschitz, continuous and integrable.
4. Splitting the integral. Let v be C-Lipschitz. By step 3, Dv(y)[Ψ(y)] = Σ_l Dv(y)[e_l]·Ψ_l(y). Each summand is measurable by step 2 and bounded by C|e_l|·|Ψ_l(y)| = C|Ψ_l(y)|, hence integrable. So ∫ Dv[Ψ] = Σ_l ∫ Dv(y)[e_l]·Ψ_l(y) dy.
5. Integration by parts. Let v be Lipschitz and fix l. By Rademacher's theorem v is differentiable at a.e. y, and there lineDeriv v y e_l = Dv(y)[e_l]. Integration by parts for a Lipschitz function against a Lipschitz compactly supported function (Mathlib LipschitzWith.integral_lineDeriv_mul_eq) then gives
 ∫ Dv(y)[e_l]·Ψ_l(y) dy = ∫ lineDeriv v y e_l · Ψ_l(y) dy = ∫ q_l(y)·v(y) dy,
 where q_l(y) := lineDeriv Ψ_l y (−e_l) = DΨ_l(y)[−e_l], since Ψ_l is differentiable everywhere. The function q_l is continuous because Ψ_l is C¹, and has compact support because DΨ_l does.
6. Apply steps 4–5 with v = u_k (K-Lipschitz by hypothesis) and v = u (K-Lipschitz by step 1). This gives ∫ Du_k[Ψ] = Σ_l ∫ q_l u_k and ∫ Du[Ψ] = Σ_l ∫ q_l u.
7. Convergence of each term. Fix l. By uniform convergence there is N with |u_k(y) − u(y)| ≤ 1 for all k ≥ N and all y. Hence |q_l(y)u_k(y)| ≤ |q_l(y)|(|u(y)| + 1) for k ≥ N. The bound is continuous with compact support, hence integrable, and q_l(y)u_k(y) → q_l(y)u(y) for every y. By dominated convergence, ∫ q_l u_k → ∫ q_l u.
8. Summing the finitely many limits of step 7 and using step 6 gives ∫ Du_k[Ψ] → ∫ Du[Ψ]. For d = 0 the sums are empty and both sides are 0. ∎

subproblem.title: Area-formula transfer of tangential pairings on an injective C¹ chart piece to a single L¹ chart field
subproblem.statement: Let P, d ∈ ℕ, V ⊆ ℝ^d open, ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P C¹ on V and injective on V with Dψ(y) injective for y ∈ V, C ⊆ V compact and Y ⊆ C Borel. Let w : ℝ^P → ℝ be integrable on ψ(Y) with respect to H^d = μHE[d], and let W : ℝ^P → ℝ^P be Borel with |W| ≤ c' such that, for H^d-a.e. x ∈ ψ(Y), W(x) ∈ Dψ(y)(ℝ^d) whenever y ∈ Y and ψ(y) = x. Then there is a Lebesgue-integrable Φ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d with Φ = 0 outside Y such that, for all β : ℝ^P → L(ℝ^P, ℝ) and α : ℝ^d → L(ℝ^d, ℝ) with β(ψ(y))∘Dψ(y) = α(y) for every y ∈ Y, ∫_{ψ(Y)} w(x)·β(x)[W(x)] dH^d(x) = ∫_{ℝ^d} α(y)[Φ(y)] dy (Bochner integrals).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P d : ℕ) (V C Y : Set (Euclid d)) (ψ : Euclid d → Euclid P) (w : Euclid P → ℝ) (W : Euclid P → Euclid P) (c' : ℝ), IsOpen V → ContDiffOn ℝ 1 ψ V → InjOn ψ V → (∀ y ∈ V, Injective (fderiv ℝ ψ y)) → IsCompact C → C ⊆ V → MeasurableSet Y → Y ⊆ C → IntegrableOn w (ψ '' Y) μHE[d] → Measurable W → (∀ x, ‖W x‖ ≤ c') → (∀ᵐ x ∂(μHE[d].restrict (ψ '' Y)), ∀ y ∈ Y, ψ y = x → W x ∈ LinearMap.range (fderiv ℝ ψ y : Euclid d →ₗ[ℝ] Euclid P)) → ∃ Φ : Euclid d → Euclid d, Integrable Φ ∧ (∀ y, y ∉ Y → Φ y = 0) ∧ ∀ (β : Euclid P → (Euclid P →L[ℝ] ℝ)) (α : Euclid d → (Euclid d →L[ℝ] ℝ)), (∀ y ∈ Y, (β (ψ y)).comp (fderiv ℝ ψ y) = α y) → ∫ x in ψ '' Y, w x * β x (W x) ∂μHE[d] = ∫ y, α y (Φ y)

Source: parent proof Step 2 (“Area measure”, “The chart field”, “Chain rule”, “Area formula for Bochner integrals”, “Ŵ ∈ L¹”) and the backward use of the area formula in Step 5; Simon Ch. 2, 3.2 and (3.5). Uses the sibling left_inverse (Lean Submission.dor_lmbsf_pwl_immersion_left_inverse). Notation: A(y) := Dψ(y), and J(y) := areaJacobianAt ψ y is the metric Jacobian (J ≥ 0, Borel by measurable_areaJacobianAt).

1. Hypotheses of the area formula.
 - Y ⊆ C ⊆ V is Borel, and ψ is injective on Y.
 - ψ is differentiable at every y ∈ Y, since V is open and ψ is C¹ on V; A(y) is injective for y ∈ Y.
 - J(y) > 0 for y ∈ Y, since J(y) = 0 iff A(y) is not injective (areaJacobianAt_eq_zero_iff_not_injective).
 - On ℝ^d, μHE[d] is Lebesgue measure (EuclideanSpace.euclideanHausdorffMeasure_eq_volume), and finrank ℝ^d = d.
2. Bochner area formula (integral_area_formula_of_injective_derivative). For every g : ℝ^P → ℝ, with no measurability or integrability assumption, ∫_{ψ(Y)} g dH^d = ∫_Y J(y)·g(ψ(y)) dy.
3. Integrability transfer (integrableOn_image_iff_integrableOn_areaJacobian_smul). Since w is integrable on ψ(Y), y ↦ J(y)·w(ψ(y)) is integrable on Y.
4. Pull-back of tangency.
 - The measure form of the area formula (map_withDensity_areaJacobian_eq) states H^d⌞ψ(Y) = ψ_#((L^d⌞Y) with density J).
 - ψ is a.e.-measurable for the latter measure: it is continuous on Y, and the density measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. L^d⌞Y. So the hypothesis on W transfers (ae_of_ae_map): for a.e. y with respect to (L^d⌞Y) with density J, the tangency predicate holds at x = ψ(y).
 - By ae_withDensity_iff, for (L^d⌞Y)-a.e. y, J(y) ≠ 0 implies the predicate at ψ(y). Since J > 0 on Y, the predicate holds at ψ(y) for L^d-a.e. y ∈ Y.
 - Taking the witness y itself gives W(ψ(y)) ∈ A(y)(ℝ^d) for L^d-a.e. y ∈ Y.
5. Chart field.
 - Let R be given by left_inverse: R is continuous on V and R(y)∘A(y) = id for y ∈ V.
 - C ⊆ V is compact and R is continuous on C, so there is M with ‖R(y)‖ ≤ M for y ∈ C (M ≥ 0 whenever C ≠ ∅).
 - Put E(y) := R(y)[W(ψ(y))]. Then |E(y)| ≤ M·c' for y ∈ Y.
 - E is a.e.-strongly measurable for L^d⌞Y: R is continuous on the Borel set V ⊇ Y, y ↦ W(ψ(y)) is a.e.-measurable on Y (W Borel, ψ continuous on V), and evaluation (T, v) ↦ T v is continuous.
6. For every y as in step 4, write W(ψ(y)) = A(y)z. Then E(y) = R(y)A(y)z = z, hence A(y)E(y) = W(ψ(y)).
7. Define Φ(y) := (J(y)·w(ψ(y)))·E(y) for y ∈ Y and Φ(y) := 0 for y ∉ Y. By steps 3 and 5, Φ is an integrable scalar times a bounded a.e.-strongly measurable field on Y. So Φ is integrable on Y, and therefore on ℝ^d. Φ = 0 off Y by definition.
8. Let β, α satisfy β(ψ(y))∘A(y) = α(y) for y ∈ Y.
 - By step 2 with g(x) := w(x)·β(x)[W(x)], ∫_{ψ(Y)} w·β[W] dH^d = ∫_Y J(y)·w(ψ(y))·β(ψ(y))[W(ψ(y))] dy.
 - For L^d-a.e. y ∈ Y, steps 4 and 6 give β(ψ(y))[W(ψ(y))] = β(ψ(y))[A(y)E(y)] = α(y)[E(y)].
 - By linearity of α(y), J(y)·w(ψ(y))·β(ψ(y))[W(ψ(y))] = α(y)[(J(y)·w(ψ(y)))·E(y)] = α(y)[Φ(y)].
 - The two integrands agree a.e. on Y, so the right-hand side equals ∫_Y α(y)[Φ(y)] dy.
9. For y ∉ Y, α(y)[Φ(y)] = α(y)[0] = 0, so ∫_Y α[Φ] dy = ∫_{ℝ^d} α[Φ] dy (setIntegral_eq_integral_of_forall_compl_eq_zero). Steps 8 and 9 prove the identity. ∎

Then for L^d-a.e. y ∈ Z, Du(y) = γ'(F(y))·DF(y), where γ'(s) := −(b − a)⁻¹ if a < s < b and γ'(s) := 0 otherwise.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: parent proof Step 4(b)–(c): the chain rule away from the kinks and the agreement lemma on the kink levels. On Z the function u is compared directly with γ∘F, so the parent's intermediate identity D(f∘ψ) = DF is not needed. Uses the sibling eqon_deriv (Lean Submission.dor_lmbsf_pwl_fderiv_eq_ae_of_eqOn), to which (DD) is passed.

1. Rademacher: u is differentiable at L^d-a.e. y (LipschitzWith.ae_differentiableAt).
2. Local form of γ (b − a > 0).
 - If s < a, then (b − s)/(b − a) > 1 and γ(s) = 1.
 - If a < s < b, then 0 < (b − s)/(b − a) < 1 and γ(s) = (b − s)/(b − a).
 - If s > b, then (b − s)/(b − a) < 0 and γ(s) = 0.
 - Moreover γ(a) = 1 and γ(b) = 0.
3. Decomposition. Z = Z₀ ∪ Z_a ∪ Z_b, where Z₀ := Z ∩ {F ≠ a} ∩ {F ≠ b}, Z_a := Z ∩ F⁻¹(a) and Z_b := Z ∩ F⁻¹(b). F is continuous, so all three sets are Borel.
4. Kink levels. On Z_a, u = γ(a) = 1. Apply eqon_deriv to Z_a, v₁ = u and the constant v₂ ≡ 1, which is differentiable everywhere with derivative 0. For a.e. y ∈ Z_a at which u is differentiable, this gives Du(y) = 0. Since F(y) = a ∉ (a, b), γ'(F(y)) = 0, so Du(y) = 0 = γ'(F(y))DF(y). The same argument with v₂ ≡ 0 = γ(b) handles Z_b.
5. Away from the kinks. Let g := γ∘F and let F(y) ∉ {a, b}.
 - By continuity of F, for z near y the value F(z) lies in the same one of the open sets (−∞, a), (a, b), (b, ∞) as F(y).
 - By step 2, near y either g ≡ 1, or g(z) = (b − F(z))/(b − a), or g ≡ 0.
 - So g is differentiable at y with Dg(y) = 0, −(b − a)⁻¹DF(y) and 0 respectively, i.e. Dg(y) = γ'(F(y))DF(y). (A function eventually equal near y to a differentiable function has the same derivative at y.)
 - u = g on Z₀ ⊆ Z, so eqon_deriv applied to Z₀, v₁ = u, v₂ = g gives Du(y) = Dg(y) = γ'(F(y))DF(y) for a.e. y ∈ Z₀ at which u is differentiable.
6. Intersect the full-measure sets of steps 1, 4 (for a and for b) and 5. For y ∈ Z in the intersection, exactly one of F(y) = a, F(y) = b, F(y) ∉ {a, b} holds, and in each case Du(y) = γ'(F(y))DF(y). ∎

With Dv(y) the Fréchet derivative (fderiv; 0 where v is not differentiable) and Bochner integrals for Lebesgue measure, ∫ Du_k(y)[Φ(y)] dy → ∫ Du(y)[Φ(y)] dy as k → ∞.

1. u is K-Lipschitz: |u(x) − u(z)| = lim_k |u_k(x) − u_k(z)| ≤ K|x − z|.
2. Uniform bound. Let v be K-Lipschitz (v = u_k or v = u) and let Θ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d be integrable.

 - y ↦ Dv(y) is Borel (measurable_fderiv). So y ↦ Dv(y)[Θ(y)] is a.e.-strongly measurable, being continuous evaluation of the pair (Dv(y), Θ(y)).
 - |Dv(y)[Θ(y)]| ≤ K|Θ(y)|. Hence y ↦ Dv(y)[Θ(y)] is integrable and |∫ Dv[Θ]| ≤ K ∫|Θ|.
 - By linearity of Dv(y) and of the integral, ∫ Dv[Φ] = ∫ Dv[Φ − Ψ] + ∫ Dv[Ψ] for every integrable Ψ.
3. Fix ε > 0 and put η := ε/(4K + 1) > 0, so that Kη ≤ ε/4. Smooth compactly supported functions are dense in L¹ (MeasureTheory.MemLp.exist_eLpNorm_sub_le with p = 1). So there is a C^∞, in particular C¹, field Ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^d with compact support and ∫|Φ − Ψ| ≤ η. In Lean, use eLpNorm f 1 = ∫⁻‖f‖ₑ and ∫‖f‖ = (∫⁻‖f‖ₑ).toReal. Ψ is continuous with compact support, hence integrable.
4. By weak_smooth applied to (u_k), u and Ψ, ∫ Du_k[Ψ] → ∫ Du[Ψ]. Choose N with |∫ Du_k[Ψ] − ∫ Du[Ψ]| < ε/2 for all k ≥ N.
5. For k ≥ N, steps 2–4 give
 |∫ Du_k[Φ] − ∫ Du[Φ]| ≤ |∫ Du_k[Φ − Ψ]| + |∫ Du[Φ − Ψ]| + |∫ Du_k[Ψ] − ∫ Du[Ψ]| < Kη + Kη + ε/2 ≤ ε.
6. Since ε > 0 was arbitrary, ∫ Du_k[Φ] → ∫ Du[Φ]. ∎
